extracted.intended_audience: students and readers studying kinematics, mechanics, and the philosophy/grammar of scientific motion
extracted.subtask_description: Pedagogical exposition from a mechanics/textbook chapter explaining curvature, its measurement, the kinematic relation between curvature and acceleration, decomposition of acceleration, and the parallelogram law for composing motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean curvature (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean curvature over an arc P4P5 is the ratio of the angle between the tangents at its extremities (L4NL5) to the length of the arc P4P5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via the curvature-chart construction (Fig. 16): plotting successive angle-units horizontally and positions vertically, drawing chords Q4Q5 whose slope to the vertical measures the mean curvature of the corresponding portion of the original curve. For a circle the mean curvature over any arc equals the inverse of the radius (i.e., independent of arc length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual curvature (limit definition and measurability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual curvature at a point is defined as the limit of the mean curvature as the element of arc becomes vanishingly small beyond the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the curvature-chart the actual curvature at P4 is the slope to the vertical of the tangent at the corresponding point Q4 of the chart; thus actual curvature is a measurable quantity at each point of any curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular measure and radian (angle unit justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular (radian) measure: the circular measure c of an angle is the ratio of the arc a subtended at the centre to the radius r of the circle; the unit of angle is the radian (arc equal to radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to relate angle-turning of tangents to arc-length and to justify that for a circle mean curvature = 1/r. (Footnote references Euclid and Clifford.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin of the tangent (rate of turning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The spin S of the tangent over a time t is the ratio of the angle turned by the tangent (e.g., L4NL5) to the time t; the actual spin at a point is the limit as t→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curvature = spin S divided by speed U (curvature = S / U). The mean spin of the tangent equals the ratio of the mean speed of the centre V to the radius IV4 in the constructed circle model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between curvature, spin, speed, and normal acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: The shunt (normal) acceleration is properly measured by the product of curvature and the square of the speed (normal acceleration = curvature × speed^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, if r is radius of curvature and U speed, normal acceleration = U^2 / r; also = S × U = r S^2 (where S is spin). The acceleration acts perpendicular to the direction of motion (in direction V4T4 in the figure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of acceleration: spurt and shunt components
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration consists of two independent components: spurt (tangential) acceleration and shunt (normal) acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spurt acceleration: along the direction of motion, measured by the rate at which speed is increased/decreased (dU/dt). Shunt acceleration: perpendicular to motion, measured by curvature × speed^2. These two are usually called speed acceleration and normal acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-acceleration consequence (straight-line uniform motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point is not accelerated, it will describe, relative to the chosen frame, a straight line with uniform speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: absence of spurt → speed uniform; absence of shunt → zero curvature → straight path. Note: neither uniform speed alone nor zero curvature alone suffices to denote absence of acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrained motion: determining normal acceleration from path and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a point is constrained to move in a given path, the normal acceleration at each position may be determined from the speed and the form of the path (i.e., its curvature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case one uses known curvature and speed to compute the normal acceleration; the problem often becomes finding speed from the tangential (spurt) acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinism of motion from initial velocity and acceleration field
rubrics_metrics.description: When a point is free to move in a plane, its motion can be theoretically determined if we know its velocity in any one position and its acceleration for all positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from normal acceleration and speed compute initial bending; use spurt to update speed for next position; iterate via small elements to construct the full path and time-chart to any desired accuracy. This yields the map of the path and the time-chart (complete description).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law for combining displacements, velocities, and accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The displacement, the mean (and in the limit actual) velocities, and the accelerations of a moving point relative to one pole/present frame are obtained by geometrically adding the corresponding vectors (parallelogram law) when changing reference pole/frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed via steps and parallelograms: the displacement of P relative to O' equals the geometric sum of displacement of P relative to O and displacement of O relative to O'. In the limit this gives that actual velocities form the three sides of a triangle and are added geometrically; an identical rule applies to accelerations. This law is the basis for synthesizing complex motions from simple component motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of motion (no absolute velocity/acceleration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute velocity and absolute acceleration are meaningless; motion is always described relative to a chosen pole/frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both pole and point have identical accelerations the relative path is unchanged. To pass between descriptions relative to different poles use the parallelogram rule; the plane-of-paper viewpoint interprets motion relative to one pole as motion about the pole plus a movement of the plane (i.e., superposed motions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature of a circle and radius of curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean curvature of a circle equals the inverse of its radius; therefore the actual curvature at a point on any curve equals 1/(radius of curvature) of the osculating circle that best fits the curve at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since a circle can be found with the same bending as the curve at a given point, its radius is termed the radius of curvature and gives curvature = 1/r. Because a circle's curvature is independent of arc length, the actual curvature at each point of a circle is constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature-chart / time-chart constructive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to visualize and construct curvature and motion: plot successive points' angle-units along a horizontal axis and positions vertically to form a curvature-chart; slopes of chords/tangents yield mean/actual curvature and permit construction of a time-chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small elements: chord slopes approach tangent slopes as elements shrink; by drawing small polygonal elements with slopes given by local speeds one can construct the time-chart to arbitrary accuracy. This constructive geometric method links the path-map and time-chart to describe motion fully.
